common_name: Saturn Seedless Grape (Crisp Red Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Saturn is a 1987 University of Arkansas release, the fourth in the program's seedless-grape series following Venus, Reliance, and Mars.

directions: Saturn is a University of Arkansas seedless table grape, released in 1987 (Plant Patent 6703) as the fourth in the program's planet-named series, bearing large, crisp, bright red berries in medium-to-large conical clusters with a mild, pleasant flavor. Vines are precocious and come into bearing early, but are only moderately winter-hardy compared with earlier Arkansas releases like Mars and Reliance, so cluster-thin young vines to avoid overcropping. Fruit ripens in late July in Arkansas trial plantings and stores reasonably well; occasional seed remnants may still be noticeable in some seasons despite the variety's seedless classification. Train to a permanent trellis and prune to spurs each winter.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture
University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service

common_name: Neptune Grape (Crack-Resistant White Seedless Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Neptune was released by the University of Arkansas in 1998 (Plant Patent 12302), the program's first yellow-green seedless table grape.

directions: Neptune is a University of Arkansas seedless table grape released in 1998 as the breeding program's first yellow-green-skinned seedless selection, from a cross of Arkansas selections 1562 and 1704. Its firm, crisp berries carry a mild, sweet, non-foxy flavor and a notably crack-resistant skin, an advantage during the humid, rain-prone ripening stretch common across the South. Vines show moderate resistance to black rot, powdery mildew, and anthracnose, though they are more susceptible to downy mildew and benefit from a basic fungicide program in wet years. Fruit ripens in early August in central Arkansas; train vines to a sturdy trellis, prune to spurs each winter, and thin crowded clusters to encourage larger berries.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Sunbelt is a 1993 University of Arkansas release (Plant Patent 8511) bred from open-pollinated Concord specifically to ripen evenly in hot Southern summers, where standard Concord often ripens unevenly.

directions: Sunbelt is a University of Arkansas juice grape released in 1993 from open-pollinated Concord, bred specifically to ripen evenly under the high summer heat of the southern United States, a trait standard Concord lacks in warm climates. The blue-black, seeded berries carry a classic labrusca, Concord-like flavor and press into juice with noticeably deeper color than Concord itself. Vines show good resistance to powdery and downy mildew with moderate resistance to black rot and anthracnose, though like most American hybrid grapes Sunbelt has no tolerance for Pierce's disease and should be sited where that disease pressure is manageable. Harvest in mid-to-late August in Arkansas trials; train to a sturdy trellis and prune to spurs each winter.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Opportunity, released in 2016, was the first white wine grape from the University of Arkansas breeding program, from a Cayuga White cross originally selected by James Moore in 1991.

directions: Opportunity was released in 2016 as the first white wine grape from the University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture's breeding program, developed from a Cayuga White cross originally selected by breeder James Moore in 1991 and later advanced by John Clark's team. It produces a neutral, food-friendly white wine with mild stone-fruit notes of peach and pear, closer in style to Chardonnay than the stronger muscat or labrusca character typical of many Southern-bred hybrids. Vines were selected for resilience to the fungal disease pressure and heat of Arkansas growing conditions, making it a practical choice for small Mid-South vineyards seeking dry white wine without the disease losses common to true Vitis vinifera. Train to a bilateral cordon system on a sturdy trellis and manage the canopy for good airflow in humid climates.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture

common_name: Enchantment Grape (Arkansas Red Teinturier Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Enchantment, released in 2016 alongside Opportunity, was the breeding program's first red wine grape, from a cross started in 1993 by John Clark and James Moore.

directions: Enchantment, released in 2016 alongside the white wine grape Opportunity, is the University of Arkansas breeding program's first red wine grape, marketed as 'Arkansas' first grape for red wine' and developed from a cross begun in 1993 by John Clark and James Moore. As a teinturier-type grape its flesh carries deep pigment along with its skin, producing a wine with an intensely dark purple color and rich, full flavor well suited to blending with lighter reds that need a color boost. Trial records show it holding up well against the fungal disease pressure typical of humid Southern summers, with only occasional light downy or powdery mildew in most seasons. Grow on a sturdy trellis with a bilateral cordon training system, pruning in late winter and thinning crowded clusters to maintain fruit quality and vine vigor.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture

common_name: Indulgence Grape (Arkansas Muscat-Flavored White Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Indulgence, released in 2021 alongside Dazzle, is a white wine grape from the University of Arkansas breeding program prized for its floral, muscat-scented wine.

directions: Indulgence is a white wine grape released in 2021 by the University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, developed alongside the related release Dazzle. Its juice produces a floral, fruity, herbal-scented wine with a pronounced muscat character, distinguishing it from the more neutral Opportunity released five years earlier from the same program. In multi-year disease trials it showed only occasional powdery mildew, a favorable record for a wine grape grown in the humid South. Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun, train to a bilateral cordon, and manage the canopy for airflow to keep disease pressure low through the humid August ripening period.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture

common_name: Dazzle Grape (Arkansas Pink Gewürztraminer-Type Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun; Dazzle, released in 2021 alongside Indulgence, is a pink-skinned wine grape from the University of Arkansas breeding program that produces a spicy, Gewürztraminer-style white wine.

directions: Dazzle is a pink-skinned wine grape released in 2021 by the University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture, developed alongside the related white wine grape Indulgence. Despite its pink skin it is pressed into a white wine with a spicy, Gewürztraminer-like aroma layered over the floral, stone-fruit character typical of the program's other recent releases. Disease trials recorded only light powdery mildew pressure in roughly two of twenty-two years of observation, a strong showing for a vinifera-type wine grape grown in the humid Mid-South. Grow on a sturdy trellis with a bilateral cordon training system, pruning in late winter and thinning fruit as needed to balance crop load with vine vigor.
sources: University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture
